slides.title: Plan for the day

slides.title: Principle and purpose
bullets: Bilirubin and its fractions are the main indicator of pigment metabolism; blood contains total, free (unconjugated) and conjugated (bound) bilirubin.
In the presence of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) bilirubin reacts with diazotised sulfanilic acid to form azobilirubin.
Without DMSO only conjugated bilirubin reacts — so the two measurements give total and conjugated bilirubin.
The colour formed is measured at 546 nm.

slides.title: Specimen and reagents
bullets: Specimen: non-haemolysed serum.
Total bilirubin: R1 — sulfanilic acid, DMSO, hydrochloric acid; R2 — sodium nitrite. Conjugated bilirubin: R1 — sulfanilic and hydrochloric acid (without DMSO); R2 — sodium nitrite.
Working reagent: 9 mL of R1 and 0.3 mL of R2 are mixed; good for 5 days at 2–8 °C in the dark.

slides.title: Specimen and reagents
bullets: Reagents are good until the date on the pack and are kept at room temperature.
The volumes, times and concentrations given belong to the kit named in the manual (Hospitex Diagnostics); with another kit follow its instructions.

slides.title: Procedure (manual)
bullets: 1. Total bilirubin: into one sample cuvette put the working reagent R1+R2 0.45 mL (1.5 mL) and sample 30 µL (100 µL); for the sample blank put R1 without R2 in the same volume with the sample. A blank and a calibrator cuvette are also prepared for the standard.
2. Mix, incubate for 10 minutes, then measure the absorbance against the sample blank. The colour is stable for 1 hour in the dark.

slides.title: Procedure (manual)
bullets: 3. Conjugated bilirubin: the same with the conjugated reagent (without DMSO), but incubate for exactly 5 minutes and measure against the blank.
4. Measuring conditions: 546 nm (530–580 nm), room temperature, 1 cm cuvette, zero — distilled water.
5. Volumes in brackets are for a standard cuvette.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Calculation: (A2 − A1) sample / (A2 − A1) standard × calibrator concentration.
Linearity up to 340 µmol/L (20 mg/dL); at higher concentrations the sample is diluted with saline and the result multiplied by the dilution factor.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Reference in the manual: total bilirubin up to 17.0 µmol/L (1.0 mg/dL); conjugated up to 5.1 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL). Each laboratory applies its own reference range.
Jaundice appears when blood bilirubin reaches 27–34 µmol/L and above.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Causes of hyperbilirubinaemia: strong haemolysis of red cells (haemolytic), impaired liver-cell function (parenchymal), impaired bile outflow (obstructive jaundice).

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Keep the incubation times exactly (10 minutes for total, exactly 5 minutes for conjugated).
Observe the shelf life of the working reagent (5 days at 2–8 °C in the dark) and the colour stability of 1 hour in the dark.
A haemolysed sample is unsuitable — take non-haemolysed serum.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Match the sample with the request form; if the result contradicts the clinical picture, check it again.
Quality control: measure a control serum in every analytical series and record the result on the control chart.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Working reagent: mix 9 mL of R1 with 0.3 mL of R2 (R1 with DMSO for total bilirubin, R1 without DMSO for direct); usable for 5 days at 2–8 °C in the dark.
The reagents are usable until the date on the pack and are kept at room temperature.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Calibration: by standard (calibrator), concentration on the vial; in the manual procedure each sample has a sample blank with R1 without R2.
Temperature is inconsistent in the source: 37 °C in the programme table, room temperature in the manual conditions — see the kit IFU.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The values belong to the Hospitex Diagnostics kit and the Screen Master Plus photometer in the manual. The IFU of the kit you use and the analyser manual always take precedence — check the parameters against them.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Serum is potentially infectious: wear gloves; never pipette by mouth.
The reagents contain acid (hydrochloric): avoid skin and eye contact; if contact happens wash at once with plenty of water and do not carry out neutralisation reactions.
Used cuvettes and tubes are disinfected.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; heel-stick blood in newborns

What it is used for: Used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find a bile duct blockage, monitor existing liver disease and check how well treatment works. It also helps diagnose disorders in which red blood cells break down too quickly, such as hemolytic anemia.

Commonly used to help diagnose newborn jaundice. Many healthy babies get it because their liver is not yet mature enough; it is usually harmless and clears within a few weeks, but in some cases high bilirubin can lead to brain damage, so infants are often tested as a precaution.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Bilirubin is a yellowish substance formed during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood, and too much can cause jaundice.

Jaundice arises in three ways: too many red cells break down (prehepatic, haemolytic); the liver is damaged or cannot process bilirubin (hepatic); bilirubin from the liver cannot reach the gut (posthepatic, obstructive — blocked bile ducts).

slides.title: Total bilirubin
cols: Possible causes of high bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia): hemolytic anemia, liver disease and blockage of the bile ducts.
So a raised total bilirubin is fractionated.
Low bilirubin (hypobilirubinemia) is not usually a cause for concern; it may be due to medicines such as antibiotics, birth control pills, sleeping pills and seizure medicines.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
cols: Mainly indirect (unconjugated) — haemolysis or impaired conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome; direct (conjugated) — hepatocellular disease (e.g., viral or alcoholic hepatitis) or cholestasis/bile-duct obstruction.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.
Interferences: An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: some medicines, certain foods and strenuous exercise can also raise bilirubin.

Limitations: Normal ranges vary between laboratories and with sex and age (infant or child). Bilirubin is only one measure of liver health; liver function tests, liver protein tests, urine tests, an ultrasound or a liver biopsy may also be needed.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

Urine and stool help tell the types apart. Prehepatic: no bilirubin in urine (unconjugated bilirubin does not pass into urine), much urobilinogen, dark stool. Hepatic: bilirubin in urine, urobilinogen often raised. Posthepatic: bilirubin in urine (dark urine), little or no urobilinogen, pale clay-coloured stool. This is a general pattern — diagnosis relies on the clinical picture and other tests.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood
What it is used for: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin is one of the names under which bilirubin blood testing is done, alongside total and indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin.
Bilirubin blood testing is used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find out whether the bile ducts are blocked and monitor existing liver disease.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Bilirubin forms during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
bullets: High: Most bilirubin circulates unconjugated. A raised conjugated (direct) bilirubin in most settings implies hepatocellular disease or biliary obstruction/cholestasis; this fraction is water-soluble and passes into urine, so bilirubin appears in urine.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.

Limitations: Bilirubin results are only one measure of liver health, and normal values vary by laboratory, sex and age (infant or child). Other tests, such as liver function tests, urine tests or an ultrasound, may be needed.

The MedlinePlus encyclopedia gives less than 0.3 mg/dL (5.1 µmol/L) as an example normal for direct bilirubin, but the reference depends on the laboratory and method — use the range on the report. Healthy urine normally contains no bilirubin.

slides.title: Prehepatic (haemolytic)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Indirect (unconjugated) ↑
Urine bilirubin: Absent — this fraction does not enter urine
Urine urobilinogen: ↑
Stool: Dark
Causes: Haemolysis; impaired conjugation (Gilbert syndrome)

slides.title: Hepatic
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Both fractions ↑, including direct (conjugated)
Urine bilirubin: Present
Urine urobilinogen: Often ↑
Markers: ALT/AST predominate (cytolysis)
Causes: Viral or alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, medicines

slides.title: Posthepatic (obstructive)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Direct (conjugated) ↑
Urine bilirubin: Present (dark urine)
Urine urobilinogen: ↓ or absent
Stool: Pale, clay-coloured
Markers: ALP and GGT predominate (cholestasis)
Causes: Bile-duct stone, tumour, stricture

slides.title: Note
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Jaundice arises in three ways: excess red-cell breakdown, liver damage, or bilirubin failing to reach the gut. This is a general scheme; diagnosis uses the clinical picture, imaging and other tests.
